title: Observational Signatures of Kerr Black Hole Lensing
comment: accepted to MNRAS, October 2026
summary: Gravitational lensing by rotating black holes is modeled, and the null geodesic equations in the strong field regime are integrated numerically. Observational signatures of the black hole spin parameter are identified by comparing image locations and shapes of extended sources at different a values. For the black hole at the center of our galaxy, angular resolutions of the order of hundreds of micro arc seconds are needed to distinguish between the true source position and gravitationally lensed image position. Angular resolution below one micro arc second is needed to determine the spin parameter of the galactic black hole using gravitational lensing.

title: Hidden Disruption in Milky Way-like Satellite Galaxy Populations
comment: 34 pages, 22 figures, submitted to OJA
summary: Determining whether a satellite galaxy is tidally disrupting from photometric observations alone remains a fundamental challenge in near-field cosmology. Cosmological simulations of Milky Way-mass galaxies predict that satellite populations should be highly disrupted, yet the observed Milky Way satellite population appears largely intact. Understanding this tension requires either uncovering disruption that has gone undetected in Milky Way satellites, or identifying limitations in the simulations themselves. We use the Auriga suite of cosmological simulations to evaluate several commonly used indicators of disruption. We find that, in the simulated satellite population, the shape, size, and proper motion alignment of a satellite's bound component are unreliable indicators of its present-day disruption state despite their widespread use in the literature. In contrast, the extended stellar distribution, specifically the ratio of stellar mass between $3r_{1/2}$ and $10r_{1/2}$ to that within $r_{1/2}$, is strongly correlated with disruption. We introduce the extended mass ratio $\mu_{\rm EMR}$ as a metric for comparing extended stellar distributions across satellites of varying masses and exploring their connection to disruption in Milky Way observations. Applying this metric to a sample of Milky Way satellites with measured extended stellar distributions, we find that many are consistent with significant ongoing disruption, even among systems traditionally classified as intact. These results suggest that tidal disruption may be substantially more widespread in the observed Milky Way satellite population than currently recognized, and establish extended stellar distributions as a promising new tool for uncovering this hidden disruption.

title: The bar-driven central complex of NGC 6946: A panchromatic and spatially resolved view of its star formation history and interstellar medium
comment: Accepted in Astronomy & Astrophysics
summary: We present a multi-wavelength analysis of the nearby spiral galaxy NGC 6946, combining optical IFS, infrared, and radio observations. We aim to characterise both the integrated and spatially resolved properties of the stellar populations and ISM, and to interpret them in the context of bar-driven galaxy evolution. We used the SED fitting code SINOPSIS to derive stellar population properties, and different prescriptions to derive ISM properties including atomic and molecular gas masses and the dust mass,temperature, and emissivity index. We find that the central 2.6 kpc hosts $40\%$ of the stellar mass, as well as the bulk of the molecular gas and dust, and has sustained enhanced star formation over cosmic time. A major star formation episode occurred 0.6 Gyr ago. The spatially resolved KS relation shows that molecular gas alone explains only part of the current SFR variance, while alternative prescriptions incorporating stellar mass and dynamical equilibrium pressure yield only modest improvements. We also find radial enhancements in the effective oxygen yield and gas mass fraction relative to surrounding regions, consistent with sustained gas accumulation. Together with the molecular gas streaming motions previously detected kinematic studies, our results are consistent with, and provide independent support for, the inward transport of gas driven by a system of nested bars and with a scenario in which a recent episode of bar-driven gas inflow enhanced the central molecular gas reservoir and sustained elevated star formation. These findings point to efficient HI-to-H$_2$ conversion, likely promoted by the combined effect of the secondary bar and the large dust content, ultimately regulating star formation. We also find indications consistent with a young stellar bar. The current decline in star formation despite large gas reservoirs suggests recent bar-driven quenching.

title: Contrasting geometries of kiloparsec-scale stellar flows associated with giant Galactic cavities
comment: 40 pages, 4 main figures and 5 Extended Data figures; Supplementary Information included
summary: Giant bubbles and cavities are widespread in star-forming galactic discs, yet the stellar dynamics associated with such structures remain poorly constrained. Here we combine Gaia Data Release 3 with three-dimensional extinction information to identify 3,502 massive-star candidates corresponding to initial masses $M_{\rm ini}\gtrsim8\,M_{\odot}$ within 5 kpc of the Sun. A search of the stellar-density field alone, independent of interstellar-medium morphology and stellar kinematics, reveals two prominent overdensities, R1 and R2, with characteristic scales of approximately 1.3 kpc. Both are subsequently found to be associated with previously identified giant interstellar cavities in projected position and line-of-sight location. After subtracting locally fitted background velocity fields, stars with full three-dimensional velocities reveal coherent divergent in-plane motions across both structures. R1 extends well beyond a known massive-star association and exhibits strongly anisotropic expansion, with one principal strain rate robustly positive and the other consistent with zero. R2 instead exhibits positive strain rates along both principal directions, indicating broadly two-dimensional internal expansion. These results show that density-selected, cavity-associated stellar structures of comparable scale can host coherent kiloparsec-scale flows with contrasting internal flow geometries and need not share a common stellar kinematic organisation.

title: The Magnetized Universe: From planet-forming disks to the high-redshift universe
comment: Part of the ALMA2040 White Paper Series. 8 pages, 2 figures
summary: The interstellar medium (ISM) is magnetized at all scales and phases in our Galaxy and other galaxies across the Universe. Spectro-polarimetric millimetre observations are essential to probe the role of the interstellar magnetic fields in the dynamics of the cold universe, and how this affects the star formation process, and planet formation in nearby star forming regions. Such observations are also essential for understanding magnetic fields in active stars and the shaping and evolution of the circumstellar environments of evolved stars. While ALMA has been revolutionary in advancing our knowledge about magnetic fields in the ISM, the limitations in calibration, especially for circular polarization, and sensitivity for large samples, have hindered robust measurements of field strengths, which are essential for fully assessing their role in ISM dynamics. An ALMA2040 that broadens spectro-polarimetric capabilities to include robust circular calibration and increases sensitivity with more collecting area will enable crucial observations of magnetic fields across the Universe and over a wide range of spatial scales to fully ascertain the influences of magnetic fields from galaxy assembly to forming planets.

title: Dust in Galaxies at $z=10-15$: Attenuation and Re-emission Predictions from the FirstLight Simulations
comment: 30 pages, submitted to ApJ on October 15, 2026. The main results are presented in Figures 9, 11, and 16. Comments are welcome
summary: Dust masses and grain properties in $z>10$ galaxies remain poorly constrained, as JWST UV attenuation and ALMA dust re-emission are rarely modelled consistently. We perform post-processed 3D dust radiative transfer on 208 snapshots of 99 galaxies at $z=10$-15 from the FirstLight simulations ($M_*=10^{6.5}$-$10^{9.5}\,M_\odot$), applying twelve dust models per snapshot (2496 runs): four dust-to-metal (DTM) prescriptions and three grain size distributions. Metallicity-dependent DTM models reproduce ALMA dust-mass upper limits at $z\gtrsim10$ and detections at $z\sim7$, as dust-to-stellar mass ratios rise sharply near $Z\sim0.2\,Z_\odot$, typically at $M_*\gtrsim10^{8.5}\,M_\odot$, where grain growth by metal accretion becomes dominant. A constant DTM of 0.4 instead violates more than half of the upper limits. For dust attenuation, SMC-like dust is favored by the observed $M_{\rm UV}$-$\beta_{\rm UV}$ relation. The observed UV slopes ($\beta_{\rm UV}\simeq-2.3$) favor small grains ($a\lesssim\lambda_{\rm UV}/2\pi\simeq0.025\,\mu{\rm m}$) producing steep UV extinction, together with a low abundance of carbonaceous grains or PAHs responsible for the 2175 $\mathrm{\mathring{A}}$ bump, consistent with silicate-rich dust. Large-grain stellar dust ($a_0=0.1\,\mu{\rm m}$) instead yields nearly grey extinction and UV slopes close to the intrinsic value ($\beta_{\rm UV,0}\simeq-2.6$). SMC and MW attenuation curves flatten at $A_{\rm V}\gtrsim0.3$, showing that relatively flat attenuation does not necessarily imply large grains. For dust re-emission, dust peak temperatures reach 60-80 K, exceeding the 40-50 K commonly assumed in ALMA dust-mass estimates. Predicted IR continuum flux increases with UV luminosity; at current ALMA sensitivities (10-20 $\mu$Jy), detections generally require $M_{\rm UV}\lesssim-21.5$. Roman wide-field surveys may identify such rare UV-bright galaxies.

title: $\texttt{GASTRO-BH}$: Effects of a Central Black Hole in GSE-like Dwarf-galaxy Mergers Around Milky Way-like Hosts
comment: 23 pages, 11 figures. Comments are welcome! Submitted to ApJ
summary: Recent evidence points to an intermediate-mass black hole (IMBH) in the most massive globular cluster of the Milky Way, $\omega$ Centauri. This globular cluster is commonly associated with the Gaia-Sausage/Enceladus (GSE) dwarf galaxy, the last major merger event of our Galaxy, as its nuclear star cluster remnant. Motivated by this, we investigate whether the interaction between a bright GSE-like dwarf galaxy with stellar mass in the range $10^{8.5}$--$10^{9.7}$ solar masses and a Milky Way-like host can either suppress or enhance the growth of a central black hole (BH) during the merger process. To this end, we perform high-resolution $N$-body and smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH) simulations with the ChaNGa framework and a modified, angular-momentum-aware Bondi-Hoyle accretion prescription, considering both isolated dwarf galaxies and merger simulations with different stellar feedback efficiencies. The merger simulations show that the interaction does not halt BH accretion; instead, tidal interactions and gas inflows during pericentric passages strongly enhance accretion, leading to BH mass growth by more than two orders of magnitude in both low- and high-feedback models. The enhanced accretion is accompanied by suppressed star formation in the dwarf galaxy. Our results suggest that mergers similar to the GSE event can efficiently fuel IMBH growth in satellite galaxies rather than suppress it. This may be in tension with the estimated low mass of the proposed IMBH in $\omega$ Centauri, but it could provide a mechanism for triggering active galactic nucleus activity in dwarf galaxies.

title: $N$-body simulations of the open cluster M67 -- I: global cluster properties
comment: 14 pages, 11 figures. Submitted to MNRAS
summary: The most recent Gaia data releases have seen the construction of many open cluster catalogues containing thousands of open clusters. Simulations of these clusters are needed in order to interpret observations, both existing and upcoming. M67 is an ideal open cluster to calibrate these simulations due to its advanced age and large, diverse binary populations. Moreover it is one of the most extensively observed open clusters with observations in several wavelengths. We aim to reproduce the global cluster properties of M67 with modern $N$-body simulations, as well as comparing its observed properties in the largest homogeneous open cluster catalogue with other available observations. We carry out several NBODY6++GPU simulations with varying initial conditions, including metallicity, half-mass radius, and the distribution of orbital binary parameters. Our models broadly reproduce the observed global properties of M67, and we are able to recreate the cluster's surface brightness profile, radial mass profile, and colour-magnitude diagram. Our favoured model indicates an initial half-mass radius of around 1.6 pc, although its total observable cluster mass may be too high. Further simulations are planned for a subsequent study, with a focus on recreating the present-day binary populations of M67.

title: How bright can a galaxy be? Extreme value predictions for high-redshift survey observables
comment: 15 pages, 10 figures. Submitted to MNRAS. Comments welcome!
summary: Assessing the significance of extreme galaxy candidates has typically relied on redshifts and stellar / halo masses inferred through inverse modelling, which carries substantial systematic uncertainty. We combine the halo mass function with a conditional model for galaxy emission and apply the Extreme Value Statistics (EVS) formalism to predict the distribution of the observed flux of the brightest galaxy expected in a given survey area, redshift interval and photometric band. We find the choice of parametric star formation history (SFH) dominates the modelling uncertainty, introducing a spread approaching $\sim 1 \, \mathrm{dex}$ by $z \sim 18$, whilst the stellar population synthesis model, initial mass function and metallicity each contribute $\lesssim 0.3 \, \mathrm{dex}$. The luminous $z \gtrsim 9$ candidates in COSMOS-Web cluster about the median prediction for the area they were drawn from, and lie at least an order of magnitude below the $3\sigma$ limit, a margin comparable to the SFH systematic. Of the observational samples reaching beyond $z \sim 13$, the two spectroscopically confirmed galaxies at $z \simeq 14$ lie close to the median prediction for their area, whereas photometric candidates at $z \gtrsim 16$ reach $+4\sigma$ (a probability to exceed of $\sim 10^{-5}$), the brightest lying at the limit obtained by converting all halo baryons into stars. Since the prediction bounds the flux far more tightly than the photometry bounds the redshift, such offsets are most naturally resolved by errors in the inferred redshifts. This approach allows extreme candidates to be assessed directly in the observational plane, making explicit the modelling assumptions common to forward and inverse approaches.

title: A new submillimeter Class I methanol maser at 345.903 GHz near the massive protostar S255IR NIRS3
comment: 6 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables
summary: We present results of further investigation of radio emission from the remarkable molecular core S255IR-SMA1 harboring a \(\sim\) 20 Msun young stellar object NIRS3 which exhibited a disk-mediated accretion burst in 2015. Our study is based on observations of this object with ALMA in Band 7 with the longest baselines, which provide an angular resolution of \(\sim\)15 mas. The obtained data reveal several spots in the bright and narrow methanol 16(1) \(-\) 15(2) A\(-\) line emission at 345.903 GHz. These spots are located close to H_2O masers, knots in the jet and arc-like structures seen in submillimeter continuum. At the same time, they are far away from the peaks of the Class II methanol maser spots. High brightness temperatures and small line widths of the 345.903 GHz line emission indicate that this emission has a maser nature. Association with the shock tracers tells that these masers belong to Class I methanol maser category. Non-LTE analysis of the physical parameters which lead to population inversion of 16(1) \(-\) 15(2) A\(-\) transition shows that some known rare Class I methanol maser transitions are also inverted under these conditions.

title: Relations between optical spectral parameters and the (far-)infrared continuum in Type~1 active galactic nuclei
comment: Accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics
summary: This study combines multi-wavelength continuum data with optical spectral properties for a far-infrared (FIR)-selected sample of Type 1 active galactic nuclei (AGNs) from AKARI data. We explore the relation between AGN physics and concomitant star formation processes using empirical correlations of optical and multiwavelength data. We measured spectral parameters including full widths at half maximum (FWHMs) and velocity shifts of broad and narrow optical emission lines, as well as continuum luminosities from GALEX FUV to AKARI 160 microns. The sample contains 88 AGNs observed at both optical and FIR wavelengths. About 50% are Seyfert 1s with both broad H$\beta$ and H$\alpha$ lines; almost all remaining objects are S1.9s with only broad H$\alpha$. The FWHMs of broad H$\beta$ and H$\alpha$ are anti-correlated with luminosity in most bands. Shifts of narrow H$\beta$, H$\alpha$, and [O III] 5007 lines and FWHM of [O III] 5007 correlate with optical and IR luminosities. Luminosities at 65 and 90 microns are more strongly connected with optical and other spectral properties than those at 140 and 160 microns. These trends extend the well-known Eigenvector 1 (EV1) correlations into the MIR and FIR domain. The anti-correlation between broad-line FWHMs and NIR and MIR luminosities is probably caused by the inclination of the torus and accretion disc: higher inclinations see less AGN radiation. However, most objects fall into Population A along the quasar EV1 main sequence, where narrower broad H$\beta$ profiles and FIR excess emission are commonly linked to higher Eddington ratios.

title: The coordinated radio and infrared survey for high-mass star formation - VI. Higher-resolution follow-up of point-like northern ultra-compact H II regions
comment: 24 pages, 12 figures
summary: The CORNISH survey provided the most complete sample of ultra-compact H II (UCHII) regions in the northern Galactic plane to date, but at its 1.5 arcsec resolution the most compact, and plausibly youngest, members of the sample could not be morphologically classified. We present Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array (JVLA) A-configuration observations at 10 GHz of 69 such CORNISH UCHII regions, reaching an angular resolution of ~0.2-0.3 arcsec and a typical rms noise of ~10 microJy/beam. All but two of the imaged targets are detected; the two non-detections lie in fields that are dynamic-range limited by bright neighbours. Six targets (~9 per cent) are resolved into pairs of sources, and a further 15 CORNISH UCHII regions detected within the fields reveal complex, multi-component structure. We also report candidate massive young stellar object (MYSO) jet knots and a row of three compact sources coincident with a previously unresolved infrared-dark H II region. The targets have a median deconvolved angular diameter of ~0.9 arcsec and physical diameters of 0.004-0.17 pc (median ~0.03 pc), with no correlation between angular size and distance, consistent with a population of intrinsically compact, young regions. Spectral indices between 1.4 and 10 GHz place ~32 per cent of the targets below the thermal free-free limit, possibly indicating non-thermal emission or variability. These data enable morphological classification of nearly the entire CORNISH UCHII sample, which will be presented in a forthcoming paper.

title: Milky Way Near Twins (MWNeTs). II. Applications of a Hierarchical Framework to NGC 3521, NGC 2903, UGC 11487, and CGCG 047-026
comment: 20 pages, 9 figures, 3 Tables, submitted to A&A
summary: Galaxies resembling the Milky Way in present-day global properties may have followed different evolutionary histories. The Milky Way Near Twins (MWNeT) framework introduced in Paper~I addresses this through seven successive stages of present-day compatibility and evolutionary diagnostics. We apply this framework to NGC~3521, NGC~2903, UGC~11487, and CGCG~047-026, spanning different levels of observational completeness and outcomes within the hierarchy. We combine archival measurements with analyses of galaxy structure, spectral-energy-distribution similarity, atomic-gas profiles, and optical nuclear diagnostics. Stages~I--IV assess environmental, structural, nuclear, and global compatibility; Stages~V--VII examine SEDs, rotation curves, and evolutionary fingerprints. We distinguish supported compatibility, partial agreement, measured incompatibility, and unconstrained diagnostics. We jointly assess these four galaxies within the MWNeT framework for the first time and derive new structural, SED-comparison, and H\,{\sc i} profile measurements for UGC~11487. NGC~2903 is a well-constrained benchmark, whereas NGC~3521 combines extensive evolutionary information with uncertain bar identification. UGC~11487 has a securely detected bar, quantitative UV--IR SED similarity, and distinctive transient nuclear tracers, but its nominal stellar mass lies below the adopted interval and its extended rotation curve remains unconstrained. CGCG~047-026 meets the initial environmental, structural, and nuclear-state criteria but remains largely unconstrained at higher stages. The four applications demonstrate the framework's ability to organise complementary evidence and identify observational priorities without equating missing data with physical incompatibility. They establish a basis for future systematic searches and for using candidate near twins as external laboratories of Milky Way evolution.

title: Inferring the delay time distribution of type Ia supernovae with CAALAM I: SED modelling choices and their effect on the delay time distribution
comment: 16 pages, 18 figures, Submitting to A&A
summary: A delay time distribution (DTD) quantifies the lag between progenitor formation and the subsequent explosive event. The DTD for a sample of Type Ia supernovae (SNe Ia) from a survey can be modelled through relative rates and the star formation histories (SFH) of all individual galaxies. Modern wide-field surveys require computationally efficient methods to model the DTD without modelling large samples of non-host galaxies. We model the DTD for a volume limited sample from SNe Ia from the Zwicky Transient Facility. The aim is to study the effect of varying SED modelling assumptions, including stellar templates, dust attenuation, SFH models, and photometric coverage. We present a new modelling framework, the Conditional Astral Ancestry Latency Analysis Machine (CAALAM), to infer the DTD of a sample of SNe Ia from the posterior of their host galaxy SFH. A model consisting of a standard stellar template, a non-parametric SFH and a flexible dust attenuation law, is favoured by the data and predicts a non-parametric DTD peaking at 100-330 Myr. When modelled as a power law, the DTD has a characteristic exponent of $-1.30 \pm 0.04$. The exponent is sensitive to dust attenuation, photometry, or SFH. When the DTD is convolved with the SFHs of the host galaxies, we find a bimodal progenitor age distribution, with $\sim60\%$ of progenitors with ages around 1.1-3.6 Gyr and the remaining progenitors older than 3.6 Gyr. We show a correspondence between the modes of the distributions of SN Ia light curve stretch and the progenitor ages. Our inferred DTD implies that most SNe Ia ($\sim 60\%$) occur promptly within 330 Myr of progenitor formation. However, the implied progenitor ages from the DTD convolved with the SFHs from our sample are significantly older. This suggests that the DTD might be a mixture of a prompt and an extended progenitor channel.

title: Comparing Infrared & X-ray-selected Active Galactic Nuclei host galaxy star formation rates to the galaxy main sequence
comment: 12 pages, 6 figures. Accepted for publication in MNRAS
summary: A key method of exploring the relationship between active galactic nuclei (AGN) and their host galaxies is to determine the astrophysical properties of galaxies that host AGN, and compare them to those that do not. Star formation rates are believed to be strongly related to nuclear activity, both indirectly via their common fuel supply, and directly via the energy injected by the AGN either suppressing or enhancing star formation. Strong observational evidence of a direct link between nuclear activity and in-situ star formation has proven elusive, likely in part due to the very different timescales of nuclear activity and episodes of star formation. To overcome these challenges, some studies have demonstrated that evidence of the aforementioned link may be found in the distributions of AGN power and star formation rates. While previous attempts to determine these distributions have largely focused on X-ray-selected samples of AGN, in this study we also attempt to determine the star formation rate distributions of infrared-selected AGN. The results vary between our samples, but at low redshift (0.8 < z < 1.2) we find that more powerful X-ray-selected AGN are more likely to occur in galaxies with higher specific star formation rates, consistent with previous studies. At higher redshifts (1.0 < z < 1.8), this trend is reversed with higher power AGN tending to occur in galaxies with lower specific star formation rates. By contrast, infrared-selected galaxies at 1.0 < z < 1.8 show no evidence of a changing star formation rate distribution with AGN power.

title: Broad Line Regions behind a Haze II: A Three-dimensional Electron-scattering Model of the Broad Br$γ$ Line in NGC 3783
comment: 24 pages, 7 figures, accepted by ApJ
summary: We investigate the broad Br$\gamma$ line in the type-1 active galactic nucleus NGC 3783 using three-dimensional Monte Carlo electron-scattering radiative transfer with SKIRT. Paper-I reproduced the observed smooth core and broad wings by convolving an intrinsic Keplerian profile with the analytic electron-scattering kernel of Laor (2006). Here we instead transport photons through explicit source and scattering geometries. For a partially covered Keplerian source, three-dimensional transfer broadens only the scattered photons and leaves an unscattered double-peaked core. For the thin Keplerian source motivated by Paper-I, a comparison of four scattering-geometry classes shows that neither a disk-like scatterer nor the tested halo variants reproduce both the core and wings. We therefore construct a two-component-source (2CS) model containing an inner Keplerian source disk, a rotating disk haze, a nearly spherical halo haze, and direct emission from a slower outer disk. A reference 2CS calculation gives Xi^2 =1.154 at i=15 deg. Polar cones with an input radial optical depth tau_hole=0.1 preserve the line profile and give a measured Thomson-thin sightline. The preferred low redistribution width, full-column ionization, and weak recombination emission cannot all be realized by a uniform thermal halo. The 2CS model is therefore a physically motivated parametric description whose medium must ultimately be tested with self-consistent radiative transfer, ionization, and dynamics.

title: Isomer-resolved ion-molecule reaction kinetics of HCO+ and HOC+
comment: accepted in A&A
summary: The HCO$^+$/HOC$^+$ abundance ratio has been observed to vary significantly in different astrophysical environments, making it an important diagnostic tool for exploring the interstellar medium. However, uncertainties in the reaction rates and branching ratios of key chemical reactions involving these ions affect the conclusions drawn from observations of either these species or other species that are derived on their basis. Here, we present isomer-resolved ion-molecule reaction rate coefficients of reactions involving HCO$^+$ and HOC$^+$ using a cryogenic ion trap experiment. We measured the rate coefficients of the isomerization reaction of HOC$^+$ to HCO$^+$ with H$_2$ and CO, as well as three different reactions producing both isomers: CO$^+$ + H$_2$ , H$_3^+$ + CO, and ArH$^+$ + CO. Our results show that the reaction of CO$^+$ with H$_2$ predominantly produces HCO$^+$ with a negligible yield of HOC$^+$ . This result is in agreement with recent theoretical predictions, but in major contrast to the generally accepted branching ratio based on previous experimental results. We also find that the isomerization reaction of HOC$^+$ to HCO$^+$ is efficient with both H2 and CO. We were able to assess the impact of our new measured reaction rate coefficients on the predicted HCO$^+$/HOC$^+$ abundance ratio using a state-of-the-art astrochemical model.

title: A precessing AGN with S-shaped morphology discovered in MALS
comment: 9 pages, 4 figures, 2 tables. Accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics
summary: We present J1221$-$1354, a precessing AGN discovered in the MeerKAT Absorption Line Survey (MALS) using deep L-band (0.9--1.6\,GHz) radio data. Its `S'-shaped morphology, revealed by the excellent surface brightness sensitivity of MeerKAT, is consistent with jet precession. Ancillary optical and infrared data establish the source as a Type 2 AGN in a moderately overdense environment. The approaching (southern) jet is brighter but shorter than the receding jet, with the northern edge of the receding jet showing a significantly younger spectral age. These features are peculiar, but consistent with a jet reorientation event in an asymmetric ambient medium, in which the jet re-enters a cavity of previously deposited plasma. A simple ballistic model yields a precession period of $P=290\pm30$\,Myr, consistent with geodetic precession in a supermassive black hole binary (SMBHB) with a binary separation of less than 1.1\,pc. We expect that deep radio continuum surveys in the near future will uncover many more such systems, helping to further strengthen the connection between jet precession and SMBHBs, and the latter's implications for the gravitational-wave background detected with pulsar timing arrays.

title: Resolving the AGN Feeding and Feedback Cycle with ALMA2040
comment: Part of the ALMA2040 White Paper Series. 10 pages, 4 Figures
summary: Understanding how supermassive black holes (SMBHs) grow and regulate the growth of their host galaxies requires tracing the cold molecular interstellar medium (ISM) throughout the full AGN feeding-feedback cycle. Molecular gas constitutes both the primary fuel for star formation and black-hole accretion and one of the ISM phases most directly affected by AGN-driven radiation, winds, and radio jets. Over the past decade, ALMA has resolved circumnuclear molecular discs, rings, spirals, tori, and jet-driven outflows on scales of tens of parsecs in nearby AGN. These studies have demonstrated that combining spatially resolved gas kinematics with multi-line diagnostics is essential for disentangling the physical processes underlying the observed gas conditions. However, our current picture remains largely based on a limited number of exceptionally nearby systems. Most local AGN have instead been observed with ALMA in a single transition at moderate or low angular resolution, preventing a systematic characterisation of both the dynamics and physical state of the gas. Moreover, existing studies have largely overlooked kinetic-mode AGN hosted by massive early-type galaxies, despite their central importance for understanding maintenance-mode feedback. In this White Paper, we argue that ALMA2040 should transform these detailed case studies into a statistical framework. A $\sim10\times$ improvement in line sensitivity relative to the current ALMA, together with fast mosaicking, ultra-wide instantaneous bandwidth, and longer baselines (resolving up to $\sim9$ mas at 230 GHz), will enable homogeneous, multi-line mapping of the molecular ISM on giant molecular clouds scales across statistically significant samples of both radiative- and kinetic-mode AGN out to $z\lesssim0.1$.

title: The environments forming stellar and planetary systems
comment: 10 pages + 1 page affiliations, 1 figure, ALMA2040 whitepaper
summary: How does a star's birth environment set the mass, angular momentum and chemical complexity delivered to its planet-forming disk, and thereby whether it builds planets, brown dwarfs or stellar companions? This requires following material from the cloud to the sub-au to few-au scales where infalling gas, magnetized winds and the disk interact, across all star-forming environments. At frequencies where young disks are optically thin, current facilities, even ALMA after its Wideband Sensitivity Upgrade, fall short by a factor of a few in angular resolution and an order of magnitude in sensitivity. Likewise, resolving how disks around distant high-mass stars fragment into tight multiples requires a linear resolution of a few to a few tens of au, currently out of reach. Yet the disks characterized so far lie almost exclusively in nearby, isolated clouds at near-solar metallicity, although the environment (radiation field, ionization rate, gas and stellar density, pressure and metallicity) varies by orders of magnitude across the Galaxy. Most stars, probably including the Sun, form in clustered regions at kpc distances, and the widest metallicity range lies farther still, in the outer Galaxy, the Central Molecular Zone and the Magellanic Clouds. With three times finer angular resolution and ten times the sensitivity, ALMA2040 will follow the path of material from cloud to disk across the full stellar-mass spectrum and, for the first time, measure how this path changes with environment: resolving the sub-au infall-impact and wind-launching zones nearby, disk fragmentation and the onset of multiplicity in distant high-mass regions, and disk formation at a few tenths of solar metallicity. It will thereby reveal the dust-obscured, embedded origins of planetary systems that optical and infrared facilities, including the ELT, see only once they emerge, and show how the birth environment shapes them.

title: Seeing Through the RFI Mask: DT-FISTA Inpainting of Pulsar Dynamic Spectra via Fourier Sparsity
comment: 14 pages, 7 figures, 1 table, comments welcome
summary: Radio frequency interference (RFI) frequently contaminates radio observations, and excising affected samples leaves masked regions in sampled images. Replacing masked samples with zero or the mean causes spectral leakage in Fourier-domain power representations. This contamination is particularly severe for modern pulsar scintillation studies, which rely on identifying and characterizing faint parabolic scintillation arcs in secondary spectra, the 2D power spectra of dynamic spectra. Scintillation arcs probe discrete scattering screens in the interstellar medium (ISM) and constrain their physical properties. However, leakage can obscure faint arcs whose power is often $<10^{-3}$ of the dominant pulsar signal power. Wiener inpainting can mitigate this leakage, but a dense implementation requires $\mathcal{O}(N^2)$ memory and $\mathcal{O}(JN^2)$ time for $N$ pixels and $J$ iterations, which is computationally expensive for full-resolution spectra containing millions of pixels. We introduce the decreasing-threshold fast iterative shrinkage-thresholding algorithm (DT-FISTA). Using a sparse Fourier representation, DT-FISTA initially estimates masked intensities from the strongest Fourier components and progressively refines them with weaker components as the soft threshold decreases. Nesterov momentum extrapolation accelerates these updates. Each iteration uses 2D fast Fourier transforms (FFT) and pointwise operations, requiring $\mathcal{O}(N\log N)$ time and $\mathcal{O}(N)$ memory. Tests on $300\times300$ pixel patches from Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical radio Telescope (FAST) observations yield lower reconstruction errors than the dense Wiener implementation, with runtime and memory requirements reduced by factors $>10^3$. Applied to full-resolution dynamic spectra, DT-FISTA suppresses mask-induced artifacts and reveals previously obscured faint arcs, enabling efficient ISM studies.

title: Resolving the AGN Feeding and Feedback Cycle with ALMA2040
comment: Part of the ALMA2040 White Paper Series. 10 pages, 4 Figures
summary: Understanding how supermassive black holes (SMBHs) grow and regulate the growth of their host galaxies requires tracing the cold molecular interstellar medium (ISM) throughout the full AGN feeding-feedback cycle. Molecular gas constitutes both the primary fuel for star formation and black-hole accretion and one of the ISM phases most directly affected by AGN-driven radiation, winds, and radio jets. However, our current picture remains largely based on a limited number of exceptionally nearby systems. Most local AGN have instead been observed with ALMA in a single transition at moderate or low angular resolution, preventing a systematic characterisation of both the dynamics and physical state of the gas. Moreover, existing studies have largely overlooked kinetic-mode AGN hosted by massive early-type galaxies, despite their central importance for understanding maintenance-mode feedback. In this White Paper, we argue that ALMA2040 should transform these detailed case studies into a statistical framework. A $\sim10\times$ improvement in line sensitivity relative to the current ALMA, together with fast mosaicking, ultra-wide instantaneous bandwidth, and longer baselines (resolving up to $\sim9$ mas at 230 GHz), will enable homogeneous, multi-line mapping of the molecular ISM on giant molecular clouds scales across statistically significant samples of both radiative- and kinetic-mode AGN out to $z\lesssim0.1$.

title: Pathfinder results for populations of planet-forming discs with SKA
comment: 9 pages, 7 figures. Published in Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII), 2026, arXiv:2026.20366 ). Report No. AASKAII/Greaves01 Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII) outlines the transformative scientific advances which will be enabled by the SKA telescopes
summary: Imaging of few-millimetre-sized dust grains (pebbles, on the construction path to planets) in protoplanetary discs has begun. The Planet-Earth Building-Blocks Legacy e-MERLIN Survey is a unique pathfinder for SKAO, imaging a sample of disc-host stars around 4.4 cm wavelength at 55 - 120 mas resolution. PEBBLeS has surveyed 10 flux-ordered fields of the northern sky, and the L1448C-N and HL Tau systems are presented as examples. The prospects for extending this science with SKAO are bright, including shorter integration times and better sensitivity to fainter outer discs. Simulations are presented of how a southern analogue to the HL Tau disc could look to SKA-Mid AA* in bands 5a and 5b. The initial lack of long baselines is suggested to pose a significant risk for imaging of planet-related features in protoplanetary discs.

title: The environments forming stellar and planetary systems
comment: 10 pages + 1 page affiliations, 1 figure, ALMA2040 whitepaper
summary: How does a star's birth environment set the mass, angular momentum and chemical complexity delivered to its planet-forming disk, and thereby whether it builds planets, brown dwarfs or stellar companions? This requires following material from the cloud to the sub-au to few-au scales where infalling gas, magnetized winds and the disk interact, across all star-forming environments. At frequencies where young disks are optically thin, current facilities, even ALMA after its Wideband Sensitivity Upgrade, fall short by a factor of a few in angular resolution and an order of magnitude in sensitivity. Likewise, resolving how disks around distant high-mass stars fragment into tight multiples requires a linear resolution of a few to a few tens of au, currently out of reach. Yet the disks characterized so far lie almost exclusively in nearby, isolated clouds at near-solar metallicity, although the environment (radiation field, ionization rate, gas and stellar density, pressure and metallicity) varies by orders of magnitude across the Galaxy. Most stars, probably including the Sun, form in clustered regions at kpc distances, and the widest metallicity range lies farther still, in the outer Galaxy, the Central Molecular Zone and the Magellanic Clouds. With three times finer angular resolution and ten times the sensitivity, ALMA2040 will follow the path of material from cloud to disk across the full stellar-mass spectrum and, for the first time, measure how this path changes with environment: resolving the sub-au infall-impact and wind-launching zones nearby, disk fragmentation and the onset of multiplicity in distant high-mass regions, and disk formation at a few tenths of solar metallicity. It will thereby reveal the dust-obscured, embedded origins of planetary systems that optical and infrared facilities, including the ELT, see only once they emerge, and show how the birth environment shapes them.

authors: Roman HLIS Cosmology Project Infrastructure Team
title: Combining Rubin and Roman photometry and its implications for photometric redshift estimation
comment: 25 pages, 18 figures, submitted to MNRAS
summary: We perform a joint Roman--Rubin photometry analysis using the LSST Science Pipelines (LSP) on simulated images, by using the Roman F158 band as the reference band and applying forced photometry on the other bands. We find that the LSP CModel photometry for Roman bands is on average unbiased, but with a bright-end systematic uncertainty floor of 7-8%. The pgauss photometry as part of the Metadetection weak-lensing shape measurement pipeline also exhibits a similar floor despite a substantially different flux-bias behavior. However, this systematic uncertainty floor becomes negligible for the color residuals and both algorithms recover unbiased colors for Roman as well as Rubin. We also show that not accounting for correlated pixel noise in Roman IMCOM coadded images results in underestimation of flux errors by a factor of ~4. Based on the measured photometry, we build a machine-learning algorithm that maps the true galaxy properties to empirical flux errors, providing a convenient method to reproduce realistic photometry errors without having to rerun expensive image simulations and photometry pipelines. We apply this empirical error model to a new mock galaxy catalog with improved realism to investigate the impact of different survey depths and configurations on photometric redshift (photo-z) estimation performance. We find that 1) Rubin survey depth significantly impacts the photo-$z$ precision, 2) additional systematic uncertainties on photometry could significantly degrade the photo-z performance especially towards high redshifts, therefore eroding the Roman--Rubin synergy, and 3) Roman photometry becomes important above z~1.5 while adding Rubin photometry to that of Roman improves photo-z performance across all redshifts. Our results provide a foundation for understanding how realistic uncertainties in galaxy photometry may propagate into the Roman--Rubin synergy in photo-z analyses.

title: The LSST Science Pipelines Software: Optical Survey Pipeline Reduction and Analysis Environment
comment: 31 pages, 8 figures, accepted for publication in the Astrophysical Journal Supplement (ApJS). Initial draft developed at this https URL )
summary: The NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory is executing the Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) as its prime mission, producing a series of data releases over the ten-year survey. The LSST Science Pipelines Software will be used to create these data releases and to perform the nightly prompt processing and alert production. This paper provides an overview of the LSST Science Pipelines Software, describing the components and their integration into pipelines that generate science-ready data products. We do not provide detailed descriptions of individual algorithms, but instead aim to show how the pipeline software is constructed and the breadth of the system. Similarly, we do not provide details of specific data products and the associated file formats.

title: The transformative power of ALMA2040 for mm-VLBI
comment: 16 pages, 3 figures. Part of the ALMA2040 White Paper Series
summary: The Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) has resolved horizon-scale emission in M87* and Sgr A*. Extending these observations to fainter black holes, multiple frequencies, and evolving structures requires greater sensitivity and new observing capabilities. We investigate how ALMA2040 could expand the scientific reach of global millimeter very long baseline interferometry (mm-VLBI), compared with ALMA's Wideband Sensitivity Upgrade (WSU). Phasing a larger ALMA array and enabling simultaneous observations across multiple ALMA bands would improve sensitivity and frequency phase transfer, providing spectral and polarimetric diagnostics of gravity, accretion flows, magnetic fields, and relativistic jets. In the configurations studied, ALMA2040 achieves sub-mJy baseline sensitivity at 230 GHz and improves prospects for faint-source imaging at 345 GHz, opening a path from individual horizon-scale targets toward population studies. Simulated observations of M87* show improved multi-frequency recovery of emission from the compact ring-like region toward the jet base, enabling studies of the accretion-jet connection. For Sgr A*, simulations of interstellar scattering mitigation yield a 27% reduction in the error of the recovered intrinsic source structure relative to the WSU configuration. Beyond black holes, these capabilities benefit geometric-distance measurements, stellar masers, compact transients, and other applications of high-resolution astrophysics. Together with rapid-response capabilities across the VLBI network, ALMA2040 could support a transition from isolated snapshots toward multi-frequency, time-resolved studies of compact sources.

title: A New AI/ML Based Image Reconstruction Technique for Hard X-ray Coded Aperture Imagers
summary: Here we demonstrate a new AI/ML based image reconstruction method for coded-aperture instruments that provides a pathway for embedded real-time use on-board spaceflight missions. Using the Swift Burst Alert Telescope (BAT) for our initial simulated demonstration, we used our new technique to replace the standard Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) based image reconstruction pipeline. In our alternative approach, we have created a neural network that maps detector counts directly to source positions using simulated responses from selected Swift Burst Alert Telescope (BAT) observations. The network combines convolutional feature extraction with attention and is trained at around 900 source counts. Under zero background noise, it achieves over 93\% exact-pixel localization accuracy with 400 detected source photons. The model maintains at least 90\% exact-pixel localization accuracy with up to 8{,}500 added background counts for sources with 900 detected photons. Within the evaluated region of BAT's field of view, these results show that source position can be recovered from sparse coded-aperture measurements in a wide-field instrument. A key feature of this technique is that explicit inclusion of the mask pattern is not required. This allows us to train the algorithm to "see" using data accumulated from an imaging system. These new non-traditional imaging techniques show substantial promise in enabling efficient imaging using non-planar geometries, which will enable new classes of hard X/$\gamma$-ray imaging systems and simultaneously improve imaging capability for currently operating instruments.

title: Multi-modal transmission forecasting for the Vera C. Rubin Observatory
comment: 54 pages, 7 figures, submitted to SPIE JATIS
summary: In the age of large automated surveys conducted at facilities like the NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory, delivering precision science goals demands highly efficient scheduling strategies that remain agile and dynamic to changing environments on the summit. On site, a variety of telemetry informs the scheduler of the best next pointing given the atmosphere's transmission. This live monitoring is provided by the Dutch Rubin Enhanced Atmospheric Monitor (DREAM) all-sky camera. Currently, dynamic scheduling uses short-term predictive algorithms, such as tracking cloud cross-correlations, to anticipate movement at short scheduling timescales. However, many of Rubin's core science objectives require survey strategies to commit to observations 20--40,min in advance (pair mode), which remains out of reach because clouds at those timescales can arrive from beyond the horizon. We developed a single monolithic multimodal strategy that folds asynchronous data from both the DREAM camera and weather satellite imagery to forecast multi-horizon sky transmission at 90,s, 5,min, 20,min, and 30,min in advance. We demonstrate that at 20-minute timescales, our model reduces transmission error by 21% and false-clear misses by 22% versus Rubin's frozen-flow tracker, and reduces false-clear misses by 26% versus persistence. We also demonstrate empirically, through ablations, that the DREAM all-sky camera provides short-horizon predictive power while satellite imagery provides long-horizon predictive power. We estimate the optimistic order-of-magnitude gain for survey efficiency improvement to be between 0.1% to 1%.

title: MIDSSAR: MId Dispersion Spectrograph for Stellar Activity Research
comment: 16 pages, 22 figures. Accepted for publication in PASJ
summary: We have developed and commissioned MIDSSAR (MId Dispersion Spectrograph for Stellar Activity Research), a novel fiber-fed, dual-band spectrograph optimized for high-cadence monitoring of stellar superflares and magnetic activity phenomena, mounted on the 3.8-m Seimei Telescope at Kyoto University Okayama Observatory. Utilizing a custom-designed volume phase holographic grating and a commercially available volume binary transmission grating, the instrument achieves simultaneous observations of key chromospheric activity indicators: the CaII H&K band (382.5-406.5nm) at a resolving power of R=13,800, and the H$\alpha$ band (641.1-667.6nm) at R=18,200. MIDSSAR is strategically integrated with the existing high-dispersion spectrograph GAOES-RV to enable concurrent photosphere-chromosphere monitoring. The control software coordinates high-speed dual-camera exposures down to 1ms while incorporating real-time telescope telemetry into the data headers. We also developed a dedicated data reduction pipeline that automatically executes calibration, spatial reconstruction of the 61-fiber bundle, and one-dimensional spectral extraction with a wavelength precision of $\sim$ 0.002nm. Initial on-sky test observations conducted from March to May 2026 successfully verified the system's quantitative readiness. The observed signal-to-noise ratio characteristics perfectly align with modeled theoretical limits under varying seeing conditions, confirming that the entire instrument complex successfully meets its primary design requirements and operational expectations for systematic stellar astrophysics surveys.

title: On the foundations of anthropic reasoning: Implications for life across the universe
comment: 12 pages, 4 figures. To be submitted very shortly
summary: With only one confirmed example, namely the Earth, the abundance of life across the universe remains deeply uncertain, and local evidence about Earth's particular circumstances can significantly shape our knowledge of life elsewhere. Such extrapolation is difficult not only because of this sample size of one, but also due to observer selection effects discussed under the Anthropic Principle. In this paper, we describe and apply a framework called Full Indexical Conditioning (FIC) for performing Bayesian inference in this situation. Inspired by, but distinct from, Full Non-Indexical Conditioning, FIC conditions on all evidence available to the reasoner while considering that this evidence could have been otherwise. We address the reference class problem associated with such reasoning, demonstrating that substantive conclusions are unaffected by the choice of reference class provided it is sufficiently large. We apply FIC to several problems in astrobiology, including the Doomsday argument, the early abiogenesis time, and our location around a G-type rather than M-type star, clarifying the foundations of these arguments. We conclude that the early abiogenesis time does not rule out pessimistic possibilities for life's abundance, and that while life around M stars may be uncommon, its temporal distribution could extend far into the future. Ultimately, FIC offers a clear conceptual framework, grounded in straightforward probability theory, for tackling problems involving anthropic selection effects.

title: Seeing Through the RFI Mask: DT-FISTA Inpainting of Pulsar Dynamic Spectra via Fourier Sparsity
comment: 14 pages, 7 figures, 1 table, comments welcome
summary: Radio frequency interference (RFI) frequently contaminates radio observations, and excising affected samples leaves masked regions in sampled images. Replacing masked samples with zero or the mean causes spectral leakage in Fourier-domain power representations. This contamination is particularly severe for modern pulsar scintillation studies, which rely on identifying and characterizing faint parabolic scintillation arcs in secondary spectra, the 2D power spectra of dynamic spectra. Scintillation arcs probe discrete scattering screens in the interstellar medium (ISM) and constrain their physical properties. However, leakage can obscure faint arcs whose power is often $<10^{-3}$ of the dominant pulsar signal power. Wiener inpainting can mitigate this leakage, but a dense implementation requires $\mathcal{O}(N^2)$ memory and $\mathcal{O}(JN^2)$ time for $N$ pixels and $J$ iterations, which is computationally expensive for full-resolution spectra containing millions of pixels. We introduce the decreasing-threshold fast iterative shrinkage-thresholding algorithm (DT-FISTA). Using a sparse Fourier representation, DT-FISTA initially estimates masked intensities from the strongest Fourier components and progressively refines them with weaker components as the soft threshold decreases. Nesterov momentum extrapolation accelerates these updates. Each iteration uses 2D fast Fourier transforms (FFT) and pointwise operations, requiring $\mathcal{O}(N\log N)$ time and $\mathcal{O}(N)$ memory. Tests on $300\times300$ pixel patches from Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical radio Telescope (FAST) observations yield lower reconstruction errors than the dense Wiener implementation, with runtime and memory requirements reduced by factors $>10^3$. Applied to full-resolution dynamic spectra, DT-FISTA suppresses mask-induced artifacts and reveals previously obscured faint arcs, enabling efficient ISM studies.

title: Understanding sub-arcsecond scale radio sources and space weather with the SKA-Low using interplanetary scintillation
comment: Published in Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII), 2026 ( arXiv:2606.20366 ). Report-no:AASKAII/Chhetri01. Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII) outlines the transformative scientific advances that will be enabled by the SKA telescopes
summary: Continuum surveys with SKA-Low will provide excellent spectral information for detected objects. However, the angular resolution it provides cannot clearly distinguish between extended radio galaxies and their sub-arcsecond scale counterparts. We have previously used an interplanetary scintillation (IPS) technique with wide field-of-view instruments (the MWA and ASKAP) to detect and study $<$0.3\arcsec\ objects. The ability to identify hundreds of compact sources from large areas of the sky using $<$5 minutes of data, and associated low computational cost makes widefield IPS a very efficient approach to identify sub-arcsecond scale objects at low radio frequencies. We aim to utilise SKA-Low's flexibility in data capture, frequency coverage and high sensitivity to develop widefield IPS technique with SKA-Low, enabling the identification of compact radio sources at angular scales more than an order of magnitude smaller than that achieved by SKA-Low's longest baselines. This capability will facilitate studies of compact source populations (e.g., AGN cores), their relationship to extended radio galaxies, AGN contributions in star-forming galaxies, identify candidates for pulsars and HI absorption, and provide a network of calibrators for direction-dependent ionospheric calibration for SKA-Low. Additionally, ground-based IPS observations are one of the very few remote sensing techniques to probe the Heliosphere which will enable SKA-Low to provide unique insights into the solar wind. Here, we present recent developments in the field of compact sources at low frequencies, their synergies with other fields of astronomy and space weather, and outline the technical developments and approaches that are necessary with the SKA-Low to realise these studies.

title: The Atmospheric Chemistry and Surface Interactions on Mars (ACSIOM) Workshop 2025
comment: ACSIOM Workshop, 2025
summary: The ACSIOM workshop was held in Cambridge from 10th-12th November 2025. Its primary aims were twofold: 1) to gather UK researchers involved in Mars atmospheric science to identify current shortcomings and challenges in the field, and 2) to discuss possible collaborations and future steps needed to maximise the research output from current and future Mars missions. Workshop attendees spanned a wide range of subjects and disciplines, from atmospheric modellers and surface scientists to experimental chemists and Earth/Venus/exoplanet scientists. One of the primary outcomes of the workshop as identified by the attendees was the need for more collaborations between these different communities. It was agreed that we currently lack sufficient interaction between disciplines and this is a key challenge we need to overcome in order to properly utilise and exploit the vast pool of martian expertise available in the UK. Modellers need reaction rates from experimentalists; experimentalists need modelling context to prioritise their experiments; geologists need modelling context to understand the features they see; modellers need geological context to constrain their results. Attendees stressed that the UK Mars community has a critical mass which is internationally recognised, and improving the communication between communities would allow significant progress to be made in martian research, allowing the UK to maintain leadership in Mars science for years to come. We highlight that this is a pivotal moment for such investments as many planetary missions, both for Mars and other terrestrial bodies, are about to be launched or are being considered in the coming years. Having a strong and close-knit community will be key to better identifying needs and capabilities in order to optimise investments in missions and to have the best scientific return possible.

title: BRISK: An accelerated wide-field imager for radio astronomy
comment: 20 pages, 10 figures
summary: Wide-field interferometric imaging with non-coplanar arrays is computationally expensive, particularly as we move towards imaging large datasets from next-generation telescopes such as the Square Kilometre Array (SKA). The dominant imaging cost arises during the gridding and degridding steps, where large $w$-terms require correction. In $w$-projection, this correction uses $w$-dependent convolution kernels whose support grows rapidly with field of view (FoV) and maximum $|w|$. In $w$-stacking, visibilities are partitioned into discrete $w$-layers, each requiring a 2D Fourier transform and image-domain phase correction; the required number of layers increases with $|w|_{\max}$ and FoV. We present BRISK (Baseline-aware Rank-compressed Interferometric Sky-imaging Toolkit), a wide-field interferometric imaging algorithm that accelerates $w$-projection by exploiting the low-rank structure of its convolution kernels. For each $w$-plane, the full 2D gridding kernel is compressed using a truncated randomised singular value decomposition (SVD), yielding a compact representation from which the SVD-compressed kernel can be reconstructed on the fly while preserving the dominant kernel energy. We benchmark memory usage, runtime, and accuracy against CASA's $w$-projection and WSClean's $w$-stacking, $w$-gridding and image-domain gridding algorithms on a simulated $15 \times 15$ grid of point sources, as well as the SKA1-Low GLEAM simulated measurement sets. BRISK runs up to 2443 times faster than CASA, and up to 132 times faster than WSClean, while maintaining a peak-flux bias of less than 1% at the largest image sizes and comparable peak memory usage.

title: The Magnetized Universe: From planet-forming disks to the high-redshift universe
comment: Part of the ALMA2040 White Paper Series. 8 pages, 2 figures
summary: The interstellar medium (ISM) is magnetized at all scales and phases in our Galaxy and other galaxies across the Universe. Spectro-polarimetric millimetre observations are essential to probe the role of the interstellar magnetic fields in the dynamics of the cold universe, and how this affects the star formation process, and planet formation in nearby star forming regions. Such observations are also essential for understanding magnetic fields in active stars and the shaping and evolution of the circumstellar environments of evolved stars. While ALMA has been revolutionary in advancing our knowledge about magnetic fields in the ISM, the limitations in calibration, especially for circular polarization, and sensitivity for large samples, have hindered robust measurements of field strengths, which are essential for fully assessing their role in ISM dynamics. An ALMA2040 that broadens spectro-polarimetric capabilities to include robust circular calibration and increases sensitivity with more collecting area will enable crucial observations of magnetic fields across the Universe and over a wide range of spatial scales to fully ascertain the influences of magnetic fields from galaxy assembly to forming planets.
